paper_title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.

sections.title: The Paradigm
sections.content: Part makes the case for second half of the endgame of AI and gives it conceptual form. Section 1 places the augmented person beside the embodied robot as form of intelligent individual in the era of Physical AI, argues that the bottleneck of personal AI has moved from the capability of the model to the coupling between model and particular person, and says why the risks of augmentation belong to the proposal. Section 2 places the proposal in coordinate system of four roles the AI has played in its relationship with person and two forms an intelligent individual can take, and locates it in seventy years of work on augmenting the human intellect. Section 3 reads the five lines of technology symbiont is built on, stating for each what it already provides and what it still lacks; the gaps form the research space of Part II. Section 4 defines the objects of the paper, introduces the cognitive gap as its invariant, lists the six properties symbiont must have, and draws the symbiosis loop that organizes everything that follows.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: . . . human brains and computing machines will be coupled together very tightly. J. C. R. Licklider, Man-Computer Symbiosis, 1960 (Licklider, 1960) For the past decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been scored on single axis: how much machine can accomplish on its own. Measured on that axis, the results are substantial. AI models now can write and review code, draft and summarize documents, search, plan, and carry out multistep tasks on computer (OpenAI, 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Anthropic, 2024a). Productivity at the desk, the part of work that takes place in front of screen, has been transformed and in large part solved. An ordinary day, however, still contains the same losses it always did, and one persons day is enough to show them. In the morning, working alone, researcher has an idea that slips away before it is written down. In the afternoon, in meeting, colleague asks about result she published three years ago, and she cannot recall the number. In the evening, facing decision, she cannot remember how she reasoned the last time she faced one like it. Two further losses belong to the same family: visitor in an unfamiliar country who does not know how to decline an invitation politely, and someone who has just failed at something, who needs one sentence from person who knows their story and receives paragraph of generic encouragement instead. The first three are failures of access, in which something the person already possesses fails to reach the moment in which it is needed, and the last two are gaps of knowledge and of support that the person cannot close alone at that moment; none of the five is failure of intelligence. In each case an AI that holds the relevant knowledge exists, and in each case it is absent from the situation: it does not know who this person is, where they are, what they are trying to do, or what they are feeling, and it has no natural way to interact and communicate with them in the moment. Sections 9.2, 8.6, and 6.6 return to the three moments of this day. Most readers already carry picture of the system that would close these gaps. In the Iron Man films, Jarvis is always present, has known its owner for years, acts while he is speaking and moving, and never asks him to stop and explain.1 The reference is useful because it allows the subject of this perspective paper to be stated in one sentence: we are concerned with how every person could have such system, and with how far beyond Jarvis such system should go. The vignette Beyond Jarvis in Section 4.2 lists six directions, of which three matter most here, and each is developed later in the paper. Jarvis sees through laboratory and suit that its owner built, whereas symbiont for everyone must see through handful of affordable external devices, and it gains channels Jarvis never had, such as physiological signals, first-person video, and the owners own account, in their own words, of what they are thinking. Jarvis mostly executes and alerts, and rarely models its owners goals, emotions, or blind spots, whereas the center of gravity of symbiont is exactly that layer of mind. And Jarvis gives almost no help with other people or other cultures, which is where symbiont is most distinctive. sections.title: 1.1 The Other Half of the Endgame
sections.content: AI is leaving the screen for the physical world, and with it comes the question of what kinds of intelligent individuals that world will contain. The answer that has drawn most of the fields attention is the embodied robot, an AI with body, senses, and goals of its own (Gemini Robotics Team, 2025; NVIDIA, 2025). We argue that the era of Physical AI will contain second kind of individual of equal importance: person whose own senses, memory, and judgment are joined to an AI that lives on their body (Section 2.2). This paper is perspective on that second kind of individual. Foundation models, world models, and methods of self-improvement enter it as enabling technologies (Section 3) and as replaceable components (Section 7.4), while the proposal itself concerns the form in which an augmented person exists and is helped. The second kind of individual also changes what progress in AI is measured against, and in this sense the endgame of AI has two halves. Artificial general intelligence (AGI) asks how intelligent the machine can be. The other half, which we call AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), asks how much intelligence machine can enable in particular person. The two are built on the same base: the same foundation model can act as an autonomous agent that completes tasks, or as cognitive symbiont that augments one human being. What differs is the object of evaluation, the mode of existence, and the relationship with the person (Figure 2). This paper is entirely about the second half, and it makes two commitments to the first. symbiont delegates errands to standard agents (Section 9.1), and it improves with every gain in the base model (Section 7.4).

sections.title: 1.2 The Bottleneck Has Moved
sections.content: A persons cognitive bandwidth is fixed. Working memory holds few items, attention goes one place at time, and day has twenty-four hours. The capability of AI on isolated tasks keeps rising, but the coupling between an AI and given person has barely changed: how much the AI knows about the person, how fast it can step in, how much it interrupts when it does, and how far the person trusts it. The result is widening gap between what model could contribute and what person actually receives (Figure 3a). The next step for personal AI is tighter coupling, and tighter coupling is different problem from larger model. The claim requires qualification, since coupling is itself built on strong base models; Section 3 describes which technologies first made coupling possible, and the paper opposes only the assumption that larger base is sufficient. Three observable symptoms mark insufficient coupling: every conversation starts by re-explaining the background, help arrives too late or too loudly, and people entrust nothing important to the system. They point, respectively, to Sections 6, 8, and 12. Figure 3b shows the mechanism by which the relationship nonetheless shifts: stronger models absorb more context, which lowers the cost of being understood, which moves interaction off the screen and onto the body, which produces new kind of context, the record of life, which makes those models more useful to that person in turn. 6 1.3 Risk and Legitimacy From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts AI capability on isolated tasks coupling between AI and person stronger base models serves this person; never trains the base new context: lifes record e unrealized augmentation relationship shifts: tool agent symbiont time (a) The bottleneck has moved interaction moves from the chat box to the body (b) Why the relationship shifts more context the AI can absorb lower cost for person to be understood Figure 3: (a) AI capability on isolated tasks keeps rising while coupling with particular person stays nearly flat; the shaded region is augmentation that is never realized. The curves are conceptual sketch, not measurements. (b) The mechanism of the shift: causal loop in which stronger base models lower the cost of being understood, move interaction onto the body, and generate new kind of context that makes the models more useful to each person in turn, without being used to train them.

sections.title: 1.3 Risk and Legitimacy
sections.content: A system that makes person more capable in front of other people raises questions that system which only completes tasks does not. When student can recall textbook during an examination, or negotiator is handed line that reads the other sides hesitation, the gain of one person is cost to another, and the other party usually does not know. The same privacy that keeps the exchange between person and their symbiont from intruding on others also hides the help from an examiner, an interviewer, or friend. Products built on this capability have already been sold for cheating, as Cluely was in 2025 (TechCrunch, 2025), and chatbot providers have switched off features for the duration of Chinas college entrance examination (Bloomberg News, 2025). Public attitudes toward cognitive enhancement are cautious, and the main objection is fairness (Pew Research Center, 2022; Faber et al., 2016). We treat these concerns as part of the proposal. symbiont differs from earlier cognitive enhancements in respect that matters for governance: it is external, removable, and inspectable, so it can follow the rules of the settings person enters and show that it did. Part IV develops the risks and the governance that follows from this property.

sections.title: 1.4 Thesis and Contribution
sections.content: Our thesis is the following. Realizing the second half of the endgame requires an AI that exists in new way: cognitive symbiont that senses what the person senses, keeps their life, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out their errands with their context in hand, and keeps learning them while both of them change. The paper develops this thesis in four parts. Figure 1 lays them out. Part (Sections 2 to 4) locates the paradigm historically and technically and gives it conceptual core. Part II (Sections 5 to 12) follows one loop from sensing to trust, in which the output of each section is the input of the next. Part III (Sections 13 and 14) asks who gains and what society of augmented individuals looks like. Part IV (Sections 15 to 18) examines what could go wrong, how augmentation can be governed, and how the claims of the paper can be measured. The contribution of the paper is the paradigm itself, taken as whole. We name second kind of intelligent individual for the era of Physical AI, the person augmented by AI, and second half of the endgame of AI, AI-augmented human intelligence, which differs from the first by its object of evaluation, its mode of existence, and its relationship with the person. We propose the cognitive symbiont as the form of system that realizes it, define it through the cognitive gap and six necessary properties, and organize its design space as symbiosis loop whose stages are each given mechanism, set of research questions, and way of being evaluated. We treat the risks of augmentation, to the person and through the person to others, as part of the paradigm, and propose that symbiont follow the rules of the settings its owner enters and be able to show that it did. We change the unit of evaluation from the AI to the augmented individual and state the open problems of the direction as research program. We propose no new algorithm; the claim of the paper is to the framing, to the organization of the design space, and to the standard of evidence it sets. Our hope is that the concept will orient new paradigm of AI research, one in which the measure of progress is how much more capable each particular person has become. 7 2. sections.title: 2 Where We Stand
sections.content: This section sets up the coordinate system used throughout the paper. The vertical axis is the relationship: four roles the AI has played with person, in the order in which each became technically possible. The horizontal axis is existence: two forms an intelligent individual can take. We then place the paper in eighty years of work on the same question and state what has changed.

sections.title: 2.1 Four Roles in Human–AI Relations
sections.content: Table 1 divides the relationship between person and an AI into four roles. Reading down the table, three properties change together. What the AI knows widens from the current message to whole life. Where the AI sits moves from chat window to computer, to the cloud, and finally onto the body. And the value it offers shifts from giving the person information, to doing tasks for them, to doing those tasks their way, to making the person themselves more capable. The first three roles share an evaluation target, the AI, and the fourth changes it to the person. The third role deserves an accurate description, since it is the closest existing relative of the fourth. The personal agents released in 2026, such as Metas Muse (Meta, 2026a), xAIs Grok Bot (GIGAZINE, 2026), and OpenAIs Dots (OpenAI, 2026), already track long-term goals, run continuously in the background, and learn preferences.2 It would be inaccurate to describe them as systems that merely complete tasks. The difference from the fourth role is one of position and purpose: personal agent acts for the person from the cloud, while symbiont thinks with the person at their side. The fourth role includes the first three. symbiont has to be competent autonomous agent and competent personal agent before it can be anything more (Section 9.1), and the four roles can coexist inside one system. We therefore read the table as four solutions to one problem under four technical conditions, and we avoid reading it as an inevitable sequence of eras.

sections.title: 2.2 Two Forms of Intelligent Individuals
sections.content: On the horizontal axis, we foresee, there are two ways for an intelligent individual to exist in the future world of Physical AI (Figure 4). An AI-augmented individual is real person who gains symbiont through wearables and other interfaces. The person remains the subject: the goals are theirs, the body is theirs, and the AI borrows their senses and their hands. An AI as individual is an embodied robot with its own body, perception, actions, and goals. The two forms matter equally for the future we describe, and this paper is concerned only with the first. Our central claim about the pair is that they share cognitive core: long-term memory, model of the situation and of other minds, timely intervention, and learning from experience. They differ in three places only: whose goals, whose body, and whose responsibility. The cognitive capabilities developed in Sections 6 to 10 therefore transfer to embodied robots, and this is the source of the paradigms generality; Section 14.2 returns to it. The third column of Figure 4, AI-driven devices in the environment, appears in the paper only as the symbionts extended reach into the physical world (Section 14.2). 2Capabilities as described at launch; we do not evaluate these products here. 8 2.3 Eighty Years of the Same Question From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts Figure 4: Two forms of intelligent individuals. Left: an AI-augmented individual, person with symbiont that senses and speaks through wearable devices. Middle: an AI as individual, an embodied robot. The two share one cognitive core, indicated by the common bar. Right, in lighter tone: devices in the environment that either form can reach into (Section 14.2). The papers scope is the left form. AI as individual is functional description and carries no claim about consciousness or legal personhood.

sections.title: 2.3 Eighty Years of the Same Question
sections.content: Using machines to augment the human intellect is an old question, and Table 2 places the paper inside that lineage. Licklider (1960) imagined people and computers thinking together in real time; Engelbart (1962) made the unit of augmentation the person together with their tools and methods; Clark and Chalmers (1998) argued that cognition can extend into external tools; Weiser (1991) and the first wearable computing researchers (Starner et al., 1997; Mann, 1997) put computing into daily life and onto the body; and lifelogging, from Bushs Memex (1945) through MyLifeBits (Gemmell et al., 2006) and SenseCam (Hodges et al., 2006), recorded life and showed that the record could support memory. More recent neighbors are egocentric AI (Grauman et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2025), mixed-initiative interaction (Horvitz, 1999; Amershi et al., 2019), just-in-time adaptive interventions in mobile health (Nahum-Shani et al., 2018), the thought-partner program of Collins et al. (2024), and the lifecycle view of context engineering (Hua et al., 2025). For each line the table records what has been settled and what we ask next, and each of those questions is taken up in later section. Our claim with respect to these lines is narrow one: none of them has taken, as its target, the augmentation of particular person across life.

sections.title: 2.4 Why Now
sections.content: Five conditions turn an eighty-year-old question into tractable research problem, and each is developed in the next section. Foundation models understand language, images, and sound and can reason over them, so that symbiont has, for the first time, brain (Section 3.1). Agent technology lets model plan, use tools, operate computer, and run for long time, so that it has hands (Section 3.2). Long-term memory, retrieval, and context management let it keep an understanding of one person across months and years (Section 3.3). World models let it begin to predict what the environment and the person will do next (Section 3.4). And wearable devices have matured to the point where first-person audio and video can be captured all day and reply can be delivered to the ear with low latency, so that the symbiont can have senses and be present (Section 3.5). What has not changed matters equally: the social infrastructure of privacy and trust, the observability of inner states, the stability of continual learning, and the cost of computing around the clock. These are the sources of Sections 12 and 17.

sections.title: 3.1 Foundation Models
sections.content: The brain of symbiont comes from four steps in the development of foundation models. Scale came first: the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), in-context learning at the scale of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020), and the scaling laws that made the next steps predictable (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Alignment made the models usable by ordinary people in ordinary language (Ouyang et al., 2022), and GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023) together with openly released weights (Touvron et al., 2023) spread the capability. Reasoning followed, from chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) to models that think before they answer (OpenAI, 2024b; Guo et al., 2025); this is what makes the slow loop of Section 8.2 possible. The fourth step is the one that matters most here. Multimodal and then omni-modal models took images into the language model (Radford et al., 2021; Alayrac et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023), then speech and video in real time (OpenAI, 2024a; Gemini Team, 2024), then any-to-any input and output (Wu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025a), and full-duplex speech models learned to listen and speak at the same time (Défossez et al., 2024). Context windows of million tokens made the inclusion of an entire day in the context window expensive rather than impossible. For symbiont, omni-modality is requirement: its input is first-person stream of sight and sound and its output is whisper or line of text, and model that only reads and writes text never reaches the scene. What foundation models lack can be stated with equal precision. They have no persistence, since each conversation starts from nothing; no sense of time; no body; and they are trained on the average person and know nothing about the one in front of them. Sections 6, 8, 5, and 7 answer these four gaps in turn.

From the bottom: wearable and embedded hardware, foundation models (one axis that runs from language to omni-modal to reasoning to world models), the personal runtime, the agentic harness, and the symbiont layer that this paper proposes. The side notes record what exists today and what the paper adds at each level. and decomposition, permissions and sandboxing, verification of results, and reusable procedural knowledge, often called skills. The same model placed in different harnesses performs very differently, fact that recurs across published results on coding agents, and it makes the harness research object in its own right. The line of work runs from interleaving reasoning with action (Yao et al., 2023), learning to call tools (Schick et al., 2023), and reflecting on failure (Shinn et al., 2023), to agents that build library of reusable skills (Wang et al., 2024), which is an early precedent for harness that improves itself (Section 10.4). Generative Agents gave agents memory stream, reflection, and planning (Park et al., 2023), which remains the closest academic prototype of an agent with life, and CoALA organized these components in the language of cognitive architectures (Sumers et al., 2024). On the engineering side, Anthropics guide to building agents argued for simple, composable patterns and for the agentcomputer interface as something to be designed (Schluntz and Zhang, 2024); SWE-agent showed that an interface built for the agent changes its performance (Yang et al., 2024); computer-use agents learned to operate any desktop or web page (Anthropic, 2024a; OpenAI, 2025b); the Model Context Protocol standardized tool access (Anthropic, 2024b); and coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex became the first autonomous agents in large-scale daily use (Anthropic, 2025; OpenAI, 2025a). In 2026 Muse and Dots pushed agents into personal life, and the Muse Gadget SDK for embedded platforms is sign that agent platforms are reaching into devices (Meta, 2026a,b; OpenAI, 2026). The benchmarks of the field all score task completion (Zhou et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Jimenez et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025; Mialon et al., 2024). For symbiont this line provides hands. Booking trip, buying something, handling desktop, writing code: todays agents can already do these, and symbiont delegates such work through its harness (Section 9.1). Beyond delegation, symbiont is new kind of harness, one organized around life instead of task (Section 11.3). Todays harnesses are task-level: they have beginning and an end, they are driven by requests, their tools are APIs, their memory is scoped to the task, and their score is completion. They have no body, no first-person senses, no model of the person, and no output that means do nothing. Sections 8, 9, and 11 take up these gaps.

sections.title: 3.3 Memory, Context, and Personalization
sections.content: Three kinds of work let model remember person. Memory systems grew from retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020) to MemGPT, which brought the tiered storage of an operating system into the model (Packer et al., 2023); to the memory stream and reflection of Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) and MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024); to A-MEM, which lets memories link to one another and evolve (Xu et al., 2025b); to Mem0, production-oriented long-term memory layer (Chhikara et al., 2025); and to sleep-time compute, which organizes memory while the system is idle (Lin et al., 2025). LoCoMo and LongMemEval measure long-conversation memory (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Context management is the second kind: Context Engineering 2.0 describes lifecycle of collecting, managing, and using context, and observes that the practice is shifting from prompting model toward managing everything long-running system knows (Hua et al., 2025); long context, cache compression, hierarchical summaries, and on-demand loading are the engineering means. Personalization is the third: LaMP measures generation tailored to user (Salemi et al., 2024); parameter-efficient adaptation makes small module per user feasible (Hu et al., 2022); test-time training and its descendants change weights during use (Sun et al., 2020, 2025; Behrouz et al., 2025); and the continual-learning literature deals with forgetting. 11 3.4 World Models Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence These are the direct foundation of Section 6 and the toolbox of Section 10, and this paper does not require new memory mechanism. What the line lacks follows from what it remembers, which is dialogue rather than life. There is no first-person stream of sight and sound, no physiology, no distinction between what the person said and what the system inferred (Section 7.2), no views that switch with the question (Section 6.4), no distinction between short-lived context and settled knowledge (Section 6.1), no consistent treatment of forgetting and deletion (Section 6.5), and the personalization it offers optimizes for sounding like the person, which is different thing from understanding them (Section 10.1).

sections.title: 3.4 World Models
sections.content: A world model is an internal model that predicts what happens next. One thread comes from reinforcement learning, where World Models and the Dreamer family plan in imagination (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2020, 2025). second is the predictive-representation route of JEPA and V-JEPA 2 (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2025). third is generative world simulation at the pixel level: Genie and Genie 3, Sora, and Cosmos (Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Brooks et al., 2024; NVIDIA, 2025). fourth is first-person data, which makes the world as seen through persons eyes learnable object: Ego4D (Grauman et al., 2022), Project Aria and its second-generation research glasses (Engel et al., 2023; Meta, 2025a), and EgoLife (Yang et al., 2025). parallel thread models people. Large foundation models show real but brittle theory-of-mind ability (Kosinski, 2024; Ullman, 2023; Strachan et al., 2024). Park et al. (2024) built generative agent for each of 1,052 real people from two-hour interview and found that the agents reproduced their participants survey answers about as well as the participants reproduced their own answers two weeks later; it is the strongest evidence to date that predictive model of particular person can be built from small amount of first-person narrative. Mental world modeling treats beliefs, intentions, and other mental variables as part of the world state itself (Fei and Zhao, 2026), which is the position this paper adopts for the mental side of the personal model (Section 7.5). For symbiont, world models provide the ability to think ahead: to predict what is about to happen around the person (an external, physical world model) and how the person will think, feel, and react, including to reminder (an internal, mental world model). Sections 7.4 and 7.5 show how both enter the personal model and why the system still stands, in degraded form, without them. Todays world models are third-person, short-horizon, and built once; the models of people are built from single interview, never updated, and unable to tell that they have gone stale.

sections.title: 3.5 Wearable and Embedded Hardware
sections.content: In three years the hardware conditions for senses and presence have changed in four places. On the head, Ray-Ban Meta glasses showed that ordinary people will wear camera and microphones all day (Meta, 2023); the Orion prototype and Meta Ray-Ban Display added display (Meta, 2024, 2025b), lightweight display glasses such as the Even G1 appeared (Even Realities, 2024), and Project Aria serves as research platform (Engel et al., 2023). On the body, pendants and recorders capture all-day audio (Mehta, 2024; Silberling, 2025; Plaud, 2024), rings and bands capture physiology, and Metas surface-EMG wristband, published in Nature, trains generic model on data from thousands of people so that new wearer can type and gesture with no calibration, and twenty minutes of personal data improve it further (Kaifosh et al., 2025). This is ready-made example of generic model with small personal adaptation on the input side, and Section 10.3 returns to it. Closer to the body, AlterEgo reads the muscle signals of silent, deliberate speech (Kapur et al., 2018), and braincomputer interfaces, noninvasive (Lévy et al., 2025) and implanted (Willett et al., 2023; Card et al., 2024), remain in research and early clinical stages. In compute, neural accelerators in phones and glasses, together with quantization and distillation, run billion-parameter models on the device (Gunter et al., 2024); low-power always-on event detection is the premise of the duty cycle in Section 5.5; and full-duplex speech models make listening while speaking feasible in latency. The counterexamples are instructive as well: the Humane AI Pin, dedicated assistant device launched in 2024, was discontinued within year (Zeff, 2025), which suggests that new device has to offer something the phone in the persons pocket does not. The first generation of senses, private output, and local compute therefore exists, and Section 5 can discuss design. What is missing can be listed: battery and heat limit what all day means, display glasses are far from shared canvas, there is no mature model from physiology to mental state, silent speech and neural interfaces are at an early stage, and above all no device has been designed as one sense of one symbiont, since each is separate product.

sections.title: 4 Conceptual Foundations
sections.content: This section gives the vision theoretical shape. We first define the objects, then state the invariant that runs through the paper, then list the properties symbiont must have and test them against the fictional reference everyone knows, and finally draw the map that organizes the research space. The pattern throughout is definition, formalization, example.

sections.title: 4.2 Six Properties and the Jarvis Test
sections.content: Table 4 lists six properties symbiont must have. Four of them, private, real-time, low-friction, and embedded, come directly from what makes the system usable in the middle of life; lifelong and proactive are added because without the first the gap cannot close across time, and without the second the person cannot ask about what they do not know they are missing. The properties pull against one another: being proactive conflicts with being low-friction, and being lifelong conflicts with being private. Those tensions are exactly the research problems of Sections 8 and 12. All day is read throughout as availability, never as continuous computation (Section 5.5). 14 4.3 The Symbiosis Loop From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts Beyond Jarvis What Jarvis already is. Jarvis passes all six properties. It has known its owner for years (lifelong); it lives in the laboratory, the house, and the suit (embedded); it reports and warns during combat (real-time); the voice inside the helmet is heard by its owner alone (private); it never asks him to stop and type or explain (low-friction); and it speaks up about incoming threats, energy, and injuries unasked (proactive). Where symbiont goes beyond it. (1) Senses. Jarvis sees through infrastructure its owner built; symbiont sees through few affordable wearables, with channels Jarvis never had (Section 5). (2) Mind. Jarvis knows schedules, systems, and the battlefield, while the center of gravity of symbiont is the owners goals, emotions, and blind spots (Section 7). (3) Cognitive help. Jarvis executes and alerts; it rarely helps its owner make life decision, recover from setback, or deal with people and cultures, which is where symbiont is most distinctive (Sections 9.2 to 9.5). (4) Growth. Across the films Jarviss understanding of its owner barely changes; symbiont must understand the person better the longer the two live together, and the whole system must evolve with it (Section 10). (5) Everyone. Jarvis is one persons bespoke system; symbiont is paradigm for all (Section 13). (6) Trust. Jarviss loyalty is given by the script; symbionts must be given by the architecture (Section 12). The subject of this paper is everyones Jarvis, six steps further on.

sections.title: 4.3 The Symbiosis Loop
sections.content: Figure 6 is the map of the research space and the table of contents of Part II. The person sits at the center. Around them runs loop: sense and interact (borrowed senses, borrowed voice, and digital traces), keep (live context, working state, and lifelong knowledge), understand (a model of the persons situation, mind, relations, and goals, built on replaceable backbone), live alongside (real-time, private, proactive participation, with silence as one of the formal outputs), act for and think with (the ladder of help from errands to thinking to social life, the help stage for short), and grow (learning from outcomes and updating the record, the model, the policy, and eventually the whole stack). Beneath the loop is the runtime that makes it run across devices and time; around it is trust, which governs authorization, privacy, correction, and exit. One feature of the figure is deliberate: the persons own words enter the record directly, without passing through inference. Of the technology lines in Section 3, agents and memory research cover mostly the keep stage and the errand end of the help stage. The weakest stages are the mental layer of understanding, the timing of participation, online learning and whole-stack evolution, and the treatment of trust as architecture. The figure is conceptual map rather than system architecture, and it does not require monolithic implementation.

sections.title: 4.4 Scope and Non-Claims
sections.content: The paper does not claim that an AI can read thoughts that were never expressed; that everyone should wear devices all day; that complete context is precondition for the system to work (Section 12.2 shows it must be useful under partial context); that symbiont outperforms the person in every domain; that the four roles of Section 2.1 are inevitable historical stages; that any one foundation model, or any one way of organizing system around it, is the only correct backbone (Section 7.4); that it proposes form of foundation model or route to general intelligence (Section 1.1); that symbiont raises trait such as intelligence or emotional skill (Section 15.3); that its use is legitimate in every setting (Section 16.2); or that any interface standard or protocol should be adopted. It claims that this is research direction worth organizing on its own, with its own invariant, properties, design space, and standard of evidence. 15 Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence

sections.content: Part II follows the symbiosis loop of Figure 6 once around the person, and each of its sections takes the output of the previous one as its input. Section 5 asks what the symbiont senses the person with and what it speaks through, since it has no body of its own. Section 6 turns the resulting streams into record with three timescales, one entry point, and many views. Section 7, the technical center of the paper, asks how that record becomes an understanding of the persons situation and mind, on backbone that can be replaced. Section 8 turns understanding into participation at the right moment, with silence as formal output. Section 9 says what the symbiont does once present, on ladder from errands to thinking to social life. Section 10 asks how the system and the person change over many rounds, up to the evolution of the whole stack. sections.title: 5 Sensing and Interacting
sections.content: The loop of Figure 6 opens with the question of what the symbiont senses the person with and what it speaks to them through. Hardware here is the symbionts borrowed body: borrowed senses on the way in, borrowed voice and borrowed canvas on the way out. The borrowed hands, devices in the environment, wait until Section 14.2.

sections.title: 5.1 Borrowed Senses, Borrowed Voice
sections.content: An embodied robot comes with eyes, ears, and mouth. symbiont has none of its own and must borrow three things: the sensors on persons body, so that it sees what they see and hears what they hear; the persons digital traces on screens, in documents, in code, and in messages; and channel of output that only the person receives, 16 5.2 The Device Constellation From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts voice in the ear, line in the glasses, picture laid over the world. Its perception is therefore first-person, incomplete, and moving with the person, and its speech is close to the ear, short, and tied to the setting the person is in. The quality of the senses sets the ceiling on understanding and the quality of the voice sets the floor on help, and neither is the goal in itself. This is also the sense in which hardware and AI are the same project, which Section 5.6 develops.

sections.title: 5.2 The Device Constellation
sections.content: No single device can carry all of this, so symbiont senses and speaks through constellation (Figure 7): glasses with first-person camera, microphones, eye tracking, and one-line display; pendant or pin that records audio and takes snapshots all day and stands in when glasses are not worn; earbuds or bone conduction for private voice output; microphone close to the mouth so that the person can speak to it at the level of breath without being overheard; ring, watch, or band for heart rate, sleep, and activity, and increasingly for EMG gestures; phone for compute and screen on the move; and desktop with authorized access to screen content, the IDE, documents, and meeting software. Each device carries role on the way in, on the way out, or both, and runtime (Section 11) manages them as one. Table 5 lists the signal sources and what each reveals about the physical and the mental side of life. Two further classes of device belong in the constellation even though they are not yet in daily use, and the first of them may become the most valuable wearable of all. Neural interfaces read the bodys own signals of intention and attention. At the surface of the body, EMG wristbands already decode the motor commands behind typing and gesture (Kaifosh et al., 2025), and electrodes in headband or around the ear record the electrical activity of the brain, in many studies with results comparable to scalp recording (Kaongoen et al., 2023); implanted interfaces, now in early clinical trials, decode attempted speech at far higher fidelity (Willett et al., 2023; Card et al., 2024). For symbiont these interfaces matter for specific reason. They are the channel through which deliberate command could one day reach the symbiont without being spoken, typed, or acted out, at lower cost to the person than any other channel. What they may read is held to the rule of every input channel (Section 5.4): commands the person directs to the symbiont, with states such as attention or fatigue read only under separate authorization. They are also the channel in which the privacy of thought (Section 12.4) is at its most literal, so the paper places them at the far end of the constellation, with the highest ceiling and the strictest conditions, and treats their maturation as part of the hardware problem of Section 17.4. The second class is the environment itself: cameras and microphones in the home, the cabin sensors and head-up display of car, the instruments of laboratory, eye-tracking contact lenses, haptic garments, and medical implants such as continuous glucose monitors. These enter the constellation on the same terms as the wearables, each with role on the way in or out, separate authorization, and management by one runtime, and they are where the symbionts senses turn into reach (Section 14.2). We therefore treat the full list of modalities in three tiers. Sight, sound, text, and digital traces are the bulk of what is usable today; physiology, motion, and gaze are collectable now and need research into their interpretation; and neural signals run from available, in surface EMG, through research, in non-invasive recording, to distant, in implanted interfaces, with the chemical senses furthest of all. Omni means that whatever signal arrives can be used; it does not require that every signal be collected.

sections.title: 5.3 Channels Out
sections.content: How the symbiont speaks to the person decides whether it can be used at all in given setting, so output deserves the same attention as input. Table 6 lists the channels, from word in the ear to picture projected into room. Three design rules follow. The strength of message must match the setting: line of text in meeting, sentence while walking, an expanded answer when the person is alone; and since the choice of channel is part of how the symbiont helps, it is one of the decision variables of the intervention policy in Section 8.4. private channel and shared canvas are different instruments: the first lets the person receive help among people without disturbing them, the second lets the person and the symbiont, or the person and other people, look at the same picture and think about it together, and this second instrument, Jarviss holographic table, earns its place in collaboration and explanation. And every channel must support retraction and update: cue that expires before delivery should never appear, and one overtaken by new information must be withdrawn (Section 8.2). The AR overlay deserves separate mention, because it is where the symbiont can draw its understanding onto the world the person sees: name and the last topic discussed next to the person in front of them, the paragraph relevant to what they are thinking highlighted on the document on the desk, route laid over street in city they do not know. Current single-eye displays with small fields of view make the first of these feasible today, and wide-field lightweight AR remains research problem.

sections.content: Privacy, as property, has two parts that the design keeps apart: what passes between the person and the symbiont belongs to the person, and its delivery can be discreet, so that the person can speak to the symbiont and hear from it 17 5.5 Always On Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence Glasses 4 (cid:215) first-person vision, mics, oneline display Earbud (cid:215) private voice out; ambient sound in Pendant / whisper mic 4 all-day audio and snapshots; your breath-level requests Ring and band 4 heart rate, sleep, activity; EMG gestures and silent input Phone > compute on the move; screen; messages and location The symbiont no body of its own; every sense and every voice is borrowed Further out AR headset projection, silent speech, neural interfaces Desktop / IDE 4 > screen content, code, documents, meetings Figure 7: The device constellation. Each device carries role on the way in (sensing, private input) or on the way out (private output, shared canvas), and often both; runtime manages them as single set of senses. The symbiont itself has no body and borrows every one of them. Neural interfaces and the devices of the environment are the far end of the constellation. without disturbing anyone nearby. On the way in, this means breath-level microphone, very short gestures (an EMG band removes the need to raise hand), and typed text; silent speech from muscle signals and neural interfaces lie further out, and the boundary we keep is the one AlterEgo marks, since it reads what person deliberately subvocalizes and nothing else (Kapur et al., 2018), rule that binds neural interface as much as microphone. On the way out, it means in-ear voice, line in the glasses, and haptic cues, with strength and content matched to the setting. Three requirements that sound alike must be kept apart. That the content of the exchange stays the persons is what the paper requires. That its delivery is discreet is capability whose use follows the setting: where setting presumes unaided performance or the sincerity of what is said, as an examination, negotiation, or an apology does, whether the person is being assisted becomes declarable fact, and declared presence is the default there (Sections 16.1 and 15.5). That device record other people without their knowledge is what the paper rejects, and Section 12.5 sets the rules.

sections.title: 5.5 Always On
sections.content: Companionship around the clock translates into system requirement of availability: the symbiont can be reached and can pick up at any moment, which is different thing from computing at full load at every moment. Battery life and latency are the two hard constraints, and the design that reconciles them is cognitive duty cycle. Most of the time only lightweight event detection runs: someone says the persons name, meeting begins, their stress rises, they whisper. An event wakes heavier computation, and the quiet hours of the night are used for offline consolidation (Section 6.3). The structure mirrors human attention, which is also not continuous. It yields three research quantities: the recall and false-alarm rate of event detection, the latency budget from an event to useful cue, and the daily energy and thermal budget. Low latency has to be written as an end-to-end budget: how many milliseconds each stage may take from sensor to model to ear, which stages can run on the device and which must go to the cloud, and which can be prepared in advance so that the fast loop of Section 8.2 finds its material ready. The duty cycle is also the first answer to the concern that round-the-clock AI depends on enormous compute; it turns the concern into an engineering quantity, and Section 11.4 completes the argument. 18 5.6 Co-Evolution of Hardware and Models From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts Table 5: Signal sources and what each reveals about the physical and the mental side of life. sections.title: 5.6 Co-Evolution of Hardware and Models
sections.content: The form of the senses will change with the capability of the models, and the training targets of the models will change with new senses. Two judgments follow from the recent record. dedicated device that adds little to the phone does not last, as the AI pin of 2024 did not (Zeff, 2025), and cognitive core without the right hardware never reaches the scene. Hardware and the core are one design problem, and Section 10.4 treats change of device as one of the ways the whole stack evolves: the person changes their glasses, and their symbiont is still theirs. 19 6. sections.title: 6 Personal Context and Lifelong Knowledge
sections.content: The senses of Section 5 deliver streams. This section asks how streams become something symbiont can use: the live context of what the person is doing now, and the knowledge that stays valid across years. The two words are not interchangeable. Knowledge is what has settled; context is what is current, from the project the person is working on this week to the scene the glasses see this second. Both must be kept, and the claim that organizes the section is that one entry point has to receive all of persons context, work and life together, for the picture of the person to be rich enough for cognitive-level help.

sections.title: 6.1 Three Timescales of One Record
sections.content: Context is information relevant to what the person is doing now. It is short-lived, high-volume, and mostly discarded once used: where this conversation has got to, which file is open in the editor and which error it stopped on, what the glasses can see and who is present, what is on todays calendar. Knowledge is what has settled out of many contexts and stays relevant across them. It is long-lived, curated, and comparatively small: facts about the person and their world, relationships, preferences, commitments, their history, the reasons they gave for things. Between the two lies third layer, working state, which lives for days or weeks: the project being pushed forward, the discussion that has not been closed, the decision due this week. The project tree in which events and projects organize one another belongs here. Two flows connect the three layers (Figure 8). Consolidation moves material upward, from context to working state to knowledge, through the filtering and merging of Section 6.3. Recall moves material downward, placing the right slice of knowledge into the context of the moment, which is exactly the step from 𝐶 ℎ 𝑡 to 𝑐𝑡 in Definition 4.2. When one word is needed for the whole we write the record. The word context is also used for the input window of language model, and in context engineering it refers to the information given to model so that the model can complete task (Hua et al., 2025). Personal context, as used here, is information about the person that is valid now, and its lifecycle serves persons life. The two meet at the recall step: injecting personal knowledge into models context window is an act of context engineering. We borrow the lifecycle view and nothing else.

sections.title: 6.2 One Entry Point for Every Context
sections.content: Table 7 lists the sources of personal context and what each sees on its own. Each sees partial person. chat assistant knows someone who asks questions, coding assistant knows programmer, desktop agent knows someone at work, and band knows body with heart rate. Questions that matter for cognitive-level help cross these boundaries: why the person was unproductive in the editor this morning (they slept five hours and the first meeting went badly), how this decision relates to the one they made six months ago, whether the stress the band sees matches the deadline the desktop sees. Only an entry point that receives every source into one record can answer such questions, and only such record supports picture of the person rich enough for the help described in Section 9. The same observation has consequence for the runtime of Section 11: it must be layer across devices and applications, and it cannot be any one application. Receiving every source is capability of the entry point and never the default for collection. Each source is authorized separately, the symbiont must be useful at low levels of authorization (Section 12.2), and the privacy column of the table exists for that reason. This is also what separates the proposal from one more memory layer: memory research records the conversations of single entry point, whereas the record here spans all of persons entry points. 20 6.3 From Streams to Record From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts Table 7: Sources of personal context, and what each sees on its own. chatbot knows questioner, coding assistant knows programmer, desktop agent knows an office worker, band knows body with heart rate. sections.title: 6.3 From Streams to a Record
sections.content: Three stages turn raw streams into knowledge. At the front, on the device and at the edge, filtering drops what is high-frequency, volatile, and not worth keeping and forwards the rest. At the back, storage absorbs frequent writes and updates and grows large. The third stage is periodic offline consolidation, which plays the role that sleep plays for human memory: in idle hours it merges the days fragments into events, files events into projects, promotes repeated patterns into stable knowledge, and demotes what has expired. Sleep-time compute and memory systems in which memories link and evolve are technical precedents (Lin et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025b), and the rhythm resolves the tension between filtering at the front and accumulation at the back. Scale forces decision about fidelity. day of first-person audio and video runs to gigabytes and life to petabytes; keeping everything is impossible and unnecessary. Raw streams are kept briefly; event-level summaries and indices of when and where something of given kind happened are kept for the long term; knowledge entries carry pointers back to their sources. The underlying difficulty is that what will matter later is unknown now, and the compromise is low-fidelity index that allows the past to be revisited. Section 17.4 lists modeling lifes record at this scale as the first open problem.

sections.title: 6.4 One Life, Many Views
sections.content: The organizing claim of the section is that the same record is projected into different views depending on the question, and that any view can be switched to at any time (Figure 9, Table 8). logic view arranges events and projects as tree that grows into graph; domain view separates work, life, family, and health; person view separates what concerns the person from what concerns others; lifetime view separates stable knowledge from passing state, which aligns with the three timescales above; chronological view orders by when something happened, when it was learned, and whether it still holds; and physical/mental view separates what happened from how it felt. Views are projections of one store: the record underneath is one, and view is generated by the question. The logic view is the main thread, and life is never forced into single tree. MyLifeBits offered multiple views for retrieval (Gemmell et al., 2006); here views also serve understanding (Section 7) and the persons own inspection and correction of what is held about them (Section 12). The paper specifies requirements on representation and retrieval and does not prescribe graph or vector store.

sections.title: 6.5 Updating, Forgetting, and Repair
sections.content: Frequent updating raises four problems: conflict, change, forgetting, and repair. Conflict between old and new is handled by keeping three times apart: when something happened, when the system learned it, and until when it holds. Change is the second, since preferences change, relationships change, and commitments are kept or cancelled, and the record has to follow them without losing the history. Forgetting, the third, comes in two kinds, decay that reduces noise and deletion that respects the persons wishes, and deleting raw record does not delete the summaries and judgments derived from it; the paper states the consistency requirement and leaves the mechanism open. Repair is the fourth. sections.title: 6.6 Remembering the Future, and the Reasons
sections.content: A record holds more than the past. It holds commitments, plans, the question to ask someone at the next meeting, decisions still forming, and the longer view of who the person wants to become. Psychology calls this prospective memory; it is the kind of memory people fail at most often, and it is where symbiont produces value most easily, by returning future intention to the working context at the right moment. It also gives the proactive help of Section 8 its most natural trigger: the system acts because the person said they would, and does not have to guess that they might want to. The record also holds reasons and not only conclusions: why the person declined that offer, why they abandoned that plan, which two options they still have not chosen between, what new evidence would make them reconsider; the third moment of the day in Section 1 is record that kept the conclusion and lost the reasons. Keeping reasons is the precondition for the decision support of Section 9.2; record without reasons can only answer questions about history. 22 6.7 The Others in Your Life From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts

sections.title: 6.7 The Others in Your Life
sections.content: A persons colleagues, family, and friends are part of their context, and symbiont has to remember where conversation with someone left off in order to support the persons social life. Those people have not authorized being modeled. We distinguish relational facts, what has happened between the person and them, which may be kept, from inferred portraits, what kind of person they are, which must be held to stricter limits than anything about the person themselves. Section 12.5 sets the boundary in detail.

sections.title: 7 Understanding a Person
sections.content: The record of Section 6 is evidence. This section asks how evidence becomes understanding of person, and it is the technical center of the paper. It runs along one line: what must be understood, where the evidence comes from, how the understanding is represented, which backbone it runs on, what world model adds to it, and where it stops. World models appear only at the fifth step, as the source of one capability, prediction.

sections.title: 7.1 What Must Be Understood
sections.content: Three objects must be understood. The first is the situation, the physical side: where the person is, whom they are with, what they are doing, what the world in front of them is about to do. The second is the mind, the mental side: the persons intention at this moment, their cognitive load, their emotion, their uncertainty, and the more stable layer of goals, values, and blind spots. The third is change: the situation changes by the minute, the mind by the hour, and the person by the year, so that the difficulty of understanding someone lies less in drawing likeness than in making the likeness move. The same experience has two faces, the event visible from outside and the persons experience of it, and the record keeps both, so the model must represent both. Mental world modeling makes the same commitment at the level of world state, treating beliefs and intentions as state variables alongside physical ones (Fei and Zhao, 2026); Section 7.5 builds on it. The third object, change, is the root of the staleness detection in that section and of the mutual growth in Section 10.

sections.title: 7.2 Two Roads to the Mind
sections.content: There are two independent sources of evidence about mind, and symbiont needs both (Figure 10). The observation road infers from behavior, choices, expression, environment, and physiology; its strength is that it sees patterns the person cannot see themselves (they do not sleep after every meeting with certain colleague), and its weakness is that one behavior has many possible causes. The self-report road takes what the person says: their account of situation, whispered sentence, correction of misreading; its strength is that only the person can say what they felt and why, and its weakness is that accounts shift with mood and flatter the teller. The two roads feed one layered model, and every entry carries its source and its uncertainty. Self-report has priority on feelings and reasons; observation has priority on patterns the person cannot see. When they disagree, the right response is to mark the disagreement, lower the weight placed on the inference, and ask when the moment is right, never to let the model overrule the person. The result of Park et al. (2024), in which agents built from two-hour interviews reproduced their participants survey answers about as well as the participants reproduced their own, shows how dense the information on the self-report road is; those agents are never updated, and that is what the symbiont adds. Most existing systems travel only the observation road, inferring preferences from interaction history, and the dedicated low-friction channel of Section 5.4 is what gives symbiont the second.

sections.title: 7.3 Layers of the Personal Model
sections.content: Table 9 gives the representation: seven layers, each with its evidence, its rate of change, and the misuse it invites, so that passing state is never mistaken for trait. The last layer, preferences about help, is new relative to the usual user profile and is the parameter source of the intervention policy in Section 8.4. One structural property of the table follows from an everyday observation: person who switches between home dialect, national language, and English changes manner, values, and even reasoning with the switch. The table is therefore indexed by context. The self at work, the self at home, and the self speaking the home dialect take different values in the identity, relations, and help-preference layers and share the experience-and-knowledge layer. The differences are not contradictions to be averaged into one personality; the models task is to recognize which self is active, from language, setting, and company, and to act with that selfs manner, weights, and social norms. Cultural psychology documents the underlying phenomenon of cultural frame switching in bicultural people (Hong et al., 2000; Ramírez-Esparza et al., 2006), and the context-indexed model is what makes the cultural help of Section 9.4 possible.

sections.title: 7.5 Two World Models
sections.content: A world model, as backbone, contributes to the personal model in two forms. An external physical world model takes the environment seen in first person as its object, scene, objects, people present, their dynamics, and predicts the next moment: the cup is about to tip, the bus is arriving, the slide is about to change. It serves help in the physical world, grounds mental cues in the situation (the person is tense because the deadline is on the screen), and supplies the extended reach of Section 14.2; its sources are the video world models and first-person data of Section 3.4. An internal mental world model takes the persons beliefs, attention, intentions, emotions, and goals as its object and predicts how they change after an event and after an action by the symbiont. It is the predictive version of the mental-state layer of Table 9, and its sources are theory-of-mind research, individual-level simulation (Park et al., 2024), and mental world modeling, which places these variables inside the world state (Fei and Zhao, 2026). The two are coupled: physical events change mental states, and mental states drive actions in the physical world. competent world model has state representation, temporal and relational reasoning, prediction of future states, prediction of the consequences of candidate actions, an expression of uncertainty, and detection of its own 25 7.6 Knowing When It Is Wrong Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence misspecification. Replace the world with this persons world and every requirement stands, and the last one matters most. sections.title: 7.6 Knowing When It Is Wrong
sections.content: It knows you better than you know yourself has three defensible meanings and one that is not. It can hold the persons whole self-context at once while they hold small part (Definition 4.2); it can see patterns across years that the person is inside of and cannot see; and it remembers the reasons they gave and have since forgotten. The fourth meaning, reading thoughts that were never expressed, the paper gives up explicitly. Two kinds of limitation must also be kept apart. Familiarity with the person and competence on the problem in front of them are different things, and system that knows someone very well may be poor at the specialist question they face this minute. The confidence of the personal model and the reliability of the backbone in that domain are estimated and reported separately; when the second is low the system narrows its advice or suggests asking person, and it never covers its ignorance of the problem with its familiarity with the person. Understanding runs both ways, since the person also learns under which conditions the system is reliable, and mutual understanding has degrees and costs; the grounding framework of Clark and Brennan (1991) describes the process without the infinite regress of each knowing what the other knows. Finally, every judgment about the person carries confidence, any of them can be overturned by sentence from the person, the system learns to ask when it is unsure, and an overturned judgment propagates through the repair of Section 6.5. Collins et al. (2024) argued that machines that think with people must model them; this section says what is modeled, on what evidence, on which backbone, and within which limits.

sections.title: 8 Living Alongside
sections.content: Understanding has to become participation at the right moment. This section turns private, real-time, low-friction, embedded presence, and proactivity that is timely, into mechanisms. It is about how the symbiont is present, when it speaks, and in what form. What it says is the subject of Section 9.

sections.title: 8.1 Two Conversations at Once
sections.content: Real-time voice assistants solved one problem: the person and the AI can speak and listen at the same time (Défossez et al., 2024). symbiont solves different one. The person is talking to another person; the symbiont is listening, thinking, and preparing at the same time, and through the private channel it hands the person line, so that the person never has to stop for it. We call this cognitive full-duplex, the real-time form of the symbiosis Licklider (1960) imagined: two conversations at once, the persons with the world and the persons with the symbiont, with the second never interrupting the first. Figure 12 shows one instance. colleague mentions figure the person reported last quarter; the slow loop retrieves it and checks it against the record; question is detected and cue appears in the glasses within second; the person answers with the figure; the topic moves on and the cue expires and is withdrawn. Four tracks run through the exchange, the external world, the persons outward expression, the private channel, and the symbionts internal state, and the figure follows them along one timeline. This capability belongs in the first usable system, since without it the symbiont is confined to the moments when the person is alone.

sections.title: 8.2 Fast Loop, Slow Loop
sections.content: Real time has two timescales, and conflating them leads to the mistaken demand that everything be low-latency. The fast loop handles the immediate: name, number, what he just said contradicts last week. The slow loop handles the background: retrieval, reasoning, updating the model, preparing summary for after the meeting. Between them sits rolling current state: what this conversation is about, who wants what, what is still unresolved. Cues must update incrementally, an updated cue must replace its predecessor, and an expired cue must disappear. The latency budget has shape. sections.title: 8.3 Implicit Intent
sections.content: Much of what person needs is never asked for. The evidence for implicit intent comes from the current activity, recent behavior, unfinished business (Section 6.6), the personal model (Section 7), and the half-sentence the person whispers. The purpose of inferring it is to have candidate help ready and to wait for suitable moment, never to decide in the persons place. When the inference is uncertain, the right move is one very short question, and the answer to that question is itself new evidence for the record; active clarification is source of context in its own right.

sections.title: 8.5 Low Friction
sections.content: Low friction means that the person never works for the help: no re-explaining the background, no reaching for phone, no switching applications, no waiting. Friction has four sources, and each is removed elsewhere in the paper: explaining the background (the record, Section 6), switching devices (the runtime, Section 11), waiting for reply (the two loops above), and tidying up afterwards (consolidation, Section 6.3). Some friction is worth preserving. Being asked one more question before an important decision, or being left to think for moment, is friction that should survive optimization (Section 10.5); interfaces that make people examine recommendation before accepting it reduce overreliance at the cost of being liked less (Buçinca et al., 2021), and that trade is the one symbiont must learn to make per person and per moment.

sections.title: 8.6 Beyond the Meeting Room
sections.content: The meeting is the first proving ground: time pressure is high, information is dense, and timing decides everything, which is why desktop copilot that analyzes meeting as it happens and feeds cues back in real time is the natural starting point. The symbiont must, however, leave the room. Three settings of presence have different rhythms and channels. Sitting at screen, in the desktop or the editor, the channel is wide and help can be expanded. In conversation, in meeting or at dinner, only line or whispered word fits. On the move, in the street, in transit, in an unfamiliar city, the earpiece and the overlay carry what the moment needs. The second moment of the day in Section 1 resolves here: the result the researcher could not recall arrives as line in the glasses while the conversation continues. What the symbiont does once present begins with doing things for the person, which is where the next section starts.

sections.title: 9 The Ladder of Assistance
sections.content: Once present, what does symbiont do? The answer is ladder with three tiers (Figure 13). At the bottom it gets things done, which is what todays autonomous and personal agents do, and symbiont must do it as well as they do and better. In the middle it thinks and feels with the person: decisions, goal formation, learning, creative work, emotional steadiness, mentorship, and psychological support within clinical limits, the settings of highest cognitive density. At the top it lives among others with the person: real-time social cognition, hard conversations, culture and dialect, and the meeting of two symbionts. Three facts organize the ladder. Each tier rests on the one below, and symbiont that cannot book flight will never be worn. Each tier up moves the object of evaluation further from task completion and closer to how the person is changed. And all three tiers run on the same machinery of Sections 6 to 8, differing only in how deep into the personal model they reach and how much intervention they are allowed (the threshold 𝜃 of Eq. (4)). One function, patient care, runs across all three tiers and receives its own treatment in Section 9.5.

sections.content: The floor of the ladder is general-purpose assistance: booking travel and hotels, shopping and comparing prices, keeping the calendar and the inbox, forms and payments, desktop work with files, slides, and spreadsheets, coding and technical work inside the editor, retrieving and organizing information, and multi-day tasks such as an application, move, or an event. symbiont does not rebuild these capabilities. The reason the same task comes out better is the record and the personal model. An agent told book my flight to the conference has to ask where the person leaves from, what they will spend, when they prefer to travel, whether they want window seat. symbiont already knows that the person has meeting on Monday morning that cannot move, that they dislike overnight flights, that they want to stay near the venue because they hope to meet particular colleague, and that the last time they took short connection they missed it. So it asks nothing, or it asks the one question that only the person can answer. One layer deeper, it knows why the person is making the trip, from the goals layer of Table 9, so it frames the task correctly and books the meeting they were hoping for alongside the flight. Table 11 works through five everyday tasks in this way, and its last column lists what can be measured: clarifying questions asked, corrections the person had to make, time to completion, how much of plan actually holds. Acting for the person is the most intrusive action in Eq. (4) and needs the firmest boundary. We propose five levels of action permission: look, suggest, draft, execute what can be undone, and execute what cannot, such as paying, sending, and committing; each level is earned along the trust curve of Section 12.2. draft composed in discussion, line rehearsed for conversation, or candidate plan never becomes an outward action or commitment on its own. Long tasks carry state, verify their results, and hand back to the person when they fail. Evaluation at this tier can keep task completion as its object as long as it adds personalization differential: the same task, the same base model, with and without the persons context, which Section 17.1 writes as Eq. (8). Current benchmarks measure the floor and say nothing about the differential (Xie et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025). We make no claim of novelty for this tier; the single claim is that the same tasks are done better with personal context, and that this can be shown.
