sections.title: 9.3 Feeling With You
sections.content: The second half of the tier runs from everyday emotion to the edge of clinical care, in four steps of increasing weight. Everyday steadiness. The small disturbances of day: remark that stung, nerves before talk, piece of bad news. The symbionts help is to be present, to know what happened, and to say the one sentence that fits, or to say 30 9.4 Relating From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts nothing and simply note it. Physiology gives early signs of stress and fatigue, and their interpretation has to remain conservative. mentor who knows your story. Useful comfort is never generic encouragement; it rests on precise understanding of the persons actual history, so that what is said touches the real point: this failure relates to those efforts and those hopes. Three levels follow. Being heard, when the symbiont restates the situation and the person thinks yes, that is it. Being understood, when it points out an attribution error the person could not see. Being moved, when it builds next step from the way the person got through similar time before. The preconditions, an established relationship of trust and general competence that in many domains exceeds an ordinary persons, are stated as conditions throughout. Psychological support within clinical limits. This is where the section has to be most careful. Relative to any mental-health application, symbiont has three advantages: it knows the persons life and does not need it retold; it is present when the trigger happens, days before the next appointment; and it can see patterns, in sleep, in social withdrawal, in language. It is therefore suited to three things: being daily practice partner for evidence-based methods such as the identification and reframing used in cognitive behavioral therapy; providing support and record between professional sessions; and recognizing early signs of relapse. It is not suited to carrying treatment on its own. For depression and anxiety the paper says that this is direction that deserves serious study, with randomized evidence for particular systems under particular conditions, from the early Woebot trial (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017) to the recent trial of generative chatbot (Heinz et al., 2025), and it does not say that these conditions can be treated by an AI. The symbionts first duty in such moments is to recognize when human professional must be brought in, with clear path for doing so when crisis signals appear, and in regulated jurisdictions this function is itself regulated, which the paper acknowledges. Habits, behavior change, and company. Long-term behavior change, in sleep, exercise, or recovery, is the home ground of just-in-time adaptive interventions (Nahum-Shani et al., 2018), and symbiont turns the phone notification into sentence from someone present. As company it can be patient and non-judging, and the risk has to be stated directly: it must never substitute for human relationships, and it should steer the person back toward people. Studies of companion chatbots show both relief of loneliness and dependence, with effects that vary with how and how much they are used (Maples et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2025). After Setback The same sentence, messed up again, and three responses symbiont might give. It listens and makes note, and says nothing. It looks back at the facts and points out what differs between this time and last time. With the persons agreement, it works through the causes and next step together with them. Three things it does not do: offer paragraph of generic encouragement; insist know you better after the person has rejected an interpretation; and continue alone when crisis signal appears.

sections.title: 9.4 Relating
sections.content: The third tier is help with people and cultures, in four forms. Real-time social cognition. meeting is one kind of social setting. In any of them the symbiont can recall the person opposite (where the conversation left off, what they care about), read the moment (the implication of what was just said, the tension between the persons argument and the others position), and help the person say it (a better phrasing, the number they forgot). Reading the moment relies on the theory-of-mind ability of large foundation models, which has shown both promise and brittleness (Kosinski, 2024; Ullman, 2023; Strachan et al., 2024), and on inferences about other people that are used only for the interaction at hand and never accumulate into portrait (Sections 6.7 and 12.5). Rehearsal and hard conversations. Practice beforehand for salary negotiation, breakup, or negative feedback to colleague; line during (the persons pace is rising; the other is really asking something else); review afterwards. simulated counterpart in rehearsal is only rehearsal and never prediction of real person. De-escalation belongs here too: the symbiont can see, in voice and heart rate, that the person is heating up before they notice, and single vibration on the private channel is enough. Relationship maintenance. This goes deeper than birthday reminder: the person has not spoken to their father in month and he mentioned medical test last time. It draws on the relations layer and on prospective memory (Section 6.6), and it is where the limits of Section 12.5 bite hardest. Language, culture, and the dialect self. Behind each language are different habits of thought and social rules. The help consists less in translation than in entering the frame: how people here greet, how they decline, what cannot be said directly. It needs the context-indexed model of Section 7.3, which knows who the person is in that language, and the online learning of Section 10.3, which learns the dialect of small place. Those two sections share one example, used here and learned there, and we avoid claims of the form language makes people more open: shifts of this kind have been reported in bicultural individuals (Ramírez-Esparza et al., 2006), and they do not license rule about any 31 9.5 Caring Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence exchange within the authorized ring visible discoverable shareable committable inner model never crosses inner model never crosses settings: chance encounter; finding someone at venue; preparing before meeting Figure 14: The symbiont handshake. sections.title: 9.5 Caring
sections.content: The function the user of symbiont may value most is one that is patient when they are not. Its core is consistency, patience, tirelessness, and noticing what people stop noticing, and it runs across all three tiers. Four settings follow; the populations themselves are treated in Section 13. In parenting, symbiont answers childs hundredth why without weariness, hands the parent sentence when the parents own temper is rising, leaves the child to the parent, and notices developmental or emotional signs worth professionals attention; the symbiont belongs to the parent, and all-day sensing of children raises separate ethical questions (Sections 13.9 and 16.7). In aging and memory decline it is memory prosthesis, who this is, whether the medication was taken, what was being looked for, with the SenseCam studies of memory-impaired patients as precedent (Berry et al., 2007); it supports orientation and safety and connects the person to family. For caregivers, the people who care for others and receive the least support, it holds the detail of care so that they can rest. In rehabilitation and chronic self-management, where the task is long, repetitive, and easy to abandon, its patience is worth most, and the handoff to clinical systems must be explicit. The failure mode common to all four is the handing over of person to machine, and in each setting the symbionts last duty is to return the person to other people.

sections.title: 9.6 Symbiont to Symbiont
sections.content: The most imaginative scene in the vision is two people, each with symbiont, in one room and not yet near each other, while their symbionts exchange cards, filter shared interests, decide whether greeting is worth it, and if so bring the two together. It is at once fanciful and practical, and Figure 14 turns it into four research questions. Which information may represent the person in an exchange, in four rings of authorization: visible, discoverable, shareable, and committable, with the inner personal model never crossing the boundary. By what criterion symbionts match, and who sets it. Whether greeting made on the persons behalf counts as their commitment. And when two symbionts each optimize for their owner, whether the outcome is good for both. Section 15.7 asks what happens when this scales to crowd. No protocol is proposed, and everything in Sections 5 to 8 stands even if symbionts never talk to each other.

sections.title: 10.2 The Personal Data Flywheel
sections.content: More authorized data gives more accurate model, which gives more useful help, which earns more trust, which brings more data. The flywheel is the core technical bet of personal AI, and in paper it is research hypothesis with two brakes. The first is echo. The symbiont influences the person, then reads the influenced behavior as evidence that the person was always like this, and the model grows ever more certain of portrait it painted itself. The remedy is to condition every update on what the system itself did: 𝑀𝑡+1 = (𝑀𝑡 ; 𝑜𝑡+1, 𝑟𝑡+1, 𝑎𝑡 ) , (5) where the update of the model 𝑀 from new observations 𝑜 and self-reports 𝑟 must take the systems own action 𝑎𝑡 as an argument; an update that ignores 𝑎𝑡 reads the result of an intervention as trait of the person. Machine learning has formal account of predictions that change what they predict (Perdomo et al., 2020). The second 34 10.3 Learning the Way Person Learns From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts brake is validation: more data does not mean truer understanding, and every round of updating has to survive the evaluation of Section 17. Growth in the person can also be the intended result of help, so change is never treated as contamination by default; what is examined is whether the evidence for an update matches the conclusion drawn from it.

sections.title: 10.3 Learning the Way a Person Learns
sections.content: A symbiont has to learn new things the way person does: in the course of life, from few experiences, incrementally, and without large offline training runs. The requirement is best stated through an example. dialect spoken in single county has no corpus and sometimes no written form; person learns it by going there, talking to people, and being corrected. symbiont needs the same ability, and it needs it under two constraints: without changing all of its parameters, through local and dynamic adjustment or no parameter change at all, and with generalization from little data. We write this as ladder of research targets, each separately testable: remember the sentences it heard; compose expressions it has learned; adapt to new speaker and accent; transfer to scenes it has not heard. Metas EMG wristband is ready-made example on the input side: generic model trained on thousands of people works for new wearer with no calibration, and twenty minutes of personal data improve it further (Kaifosh et al., 2025). generic model with small personal adaptation is the learning curve this section argues for, with the object changed from gestures to dialect and mind. Test-time training (Sun et al., 2020, 2025) and memory layers that learn at test time (Behrouz et al., 2025) are the technical lineage, and several leading researchers have named continual, sample-efficient learning as the next frontier; the paper fixes requirements and validation levels and chooses no particular route. Learning Dialect by Living There The symbiont accompanies the person to their hometown. Over few days it learns common expressions from their conversations with relatives, confirms the meanings with them, tries to understand and to help them respond the next time, and adjusts when corrected. The vignette is written to separate what memory alone can do from what requires changing the model, and to say how one would tell it remembered the sentences from it learned the dialect.

sections.title: 10.4 Evolving the Whole Stack
sections.content: As understanding of the person deepens, the base model, the harness, and the hardware must all evolve, along three routes that share one set of constraints (Figure 16). Base model upgrades. The foundation model changes every few months (Section 3.1), and the symbiont cannot be reset with it. The requirement is the information-level interface of Section 7.4: the record, the personal model, the intervention policy, and the harness configuration are defined outside the backbone, migrate when it changes, and are recalibrated during transition period, since new backbone may estimate the same evidence differently. This is the papers answer to whether symbiont needs its own private model: what must belong to the person is the record and the model of them, and it is the relationship, and never the weights, that persists. The films give the failure case; when its owner moved from Jarvis to successor system, the relationship started over. Self-improvement of the harness. symbiont may rewrite the way it works: fix routine for something the person does often, write tool, accumulate skills in the manner of skill library (Wang et al., 2024), rebalance the fast and slow loops, retune the parameters of the intervention policy. This is self-improvement in bounded form. What changes is the harness, which is readable, auditable, and reversible, and every change leaves record; the models own parameters change only by exception. Hardware generations. New glasses, new band, or new channel let the symbiont see and say little more. The record and the model are bound to no device, and what has to be relearned after change is only which channel works in which setting, never who the person is, which is the mechanism behind the co-evolution of Section 5.6. The shared constraints are four: portability (change any layer and the relationship survives), auditability (what changed and why, visible to the person), reversibility (a bad change can be rolled back), and the echo brake at system level (what the system observes after changing itself cannot be read directly as the person). One more direction follows: the better the symbiont knows the person, the more specialized its procedures should become and the fewer generic defaults it should keep, and since specialization erodes general ability, path back to the generic must be kept open, which is the system-side counterpart of the persons right to do things themselves in the next subsection.

Three changes are possible: the person learns something, which is gain; they stop practising what they have handed over, which is gain or loss depending on whether they wanted to keep it; and their preferences are slowly shaped by the system, which has to be watched. sections.title: 11 The Personal Runtime
sections.content: Everything in the previous six sections has to run somewhere. This is the layer that, in the stack of Figure 5, sits between the foundation models and the agentic harness, and that may in time grow into an AI-native operating system. We call it runtime and do not propose to rewrite an operating system.

sections.title: 11.1 Beyond an App
sections.content: A symbiont needs persistent state across devices, single permission model, scheduling of several senses and several output channels, management of the fast and slow loops, delegation to standard agents, and the one entry point for every context of Section 6.2. These requirements exceed any single application and fall short of new kernel. The personal runtime is the layer that meets them, and it can grow over time into the AI-native operating system of our vision, once enough devices and applications treat it as their entry point.

sections.title: 11.2 Layers
sections.content: Figure 17 expands the upper part of Figure 5. From the bottom: the device constellation; base capabilities, shared omni-modal model, world model, and small on-device models, all replaceable; runtime services, identity, permissions, device abstraction, continuity, the attention budget, and entry-point aggregation; the harness, which plans, uses tools, delegates to standard agents, schedules the two loops, and holds the procedures and skills it has written for itself; and at the top the record and the personal model, which are bound to no backbone and are portable. The trust layer of Section 12 runs through all of them. Two points organize the figure: the base is replaceable and the record and model are never replaced, and the harness and the runtime divide the labor, the first getting things done and the second making them happen on the right device, with the right permission, at the right time.

sections.title: 11.3 A Harness for a Life
sections.content: Current harnesses are designed around task (Section 3.2): it begins and ends, its input is span of text, its tools are APIs. symbionts harness faces life: nothing begins or ends, the input is continuous multimodal stream, the tools include persons senses and the devices around them, memory is first-class component, and most of the time the correct output is nothing at all. Six requirements follow, and the paper states them without specification: event-driven operation; the record and the personal model as native components; output channels matched to the setting; delegation to standard agents and reclamation of control from them (Section 9.1); log of the systems own actions, which the echo brake of Section 10.2 needs; and the ability to rewrite itself under audit, which Section 10.4 needs. sections.title: 11.4 The Cost of Always-On Cognition
sections.content: AI that computes around the clock depends heavily on compute and infrastructure, and the question of what happens when AI compute becomes cheap infrastructure deserves direct answer. Cost has structure that can be optimized. Most of the time lightweight on-device model does nothing but detect events; few events wake heavy model, on the device or in the cloud; the night is used for consolidation. Three research quantities follow: the compute budget per person per day, the leverage of event detection on total cost, and the effect of the split between local and cloud on privacy and latency. Whether the paradigm is economical depends on the duty cycle and not on model size. If inference costs keep falling at the rate of recent years and on-device models keep improving, one always-on symbiont per person becomes affordable before it becomes trusted, and the bottleneck moves once more, to Section 12.

sections.title: 11.5 Continuity
sections.content: Continuity is the runtimes central duty, in three forms. Across devices: what the person started at the desk continues when they walk out the door. Across interruptions: when battery dies, the person switches off collection, or the network drops, the system knows which stretch it missed and, on recovery, does not pretend to have been there. Across upgrades: when the base model or the device changes, the persons symbiont is still theirs (Section 10.4). The second form is the most often forgotten and the most damaging to trust when it fails.

sections.title: 12 Trust
sections.content: By what right does system enter persons life? The judgment that organizes this section is that the largest obstacle to symbiont, ahead of any technical one, is whether people will find it safe enough to open their whole context to it, the physical and the mental alike. Trust is therefore treated as part of the architecture. This section is about design; the risks that design does not remove, and their governance, are the subject of Part IV.

sections.title: 12.1 Trust Is the Adoption Problem
sections.content: A symbiont asks for authorization without precedent. It sees what the person sees, hears what they hear, keeps their life, infers their thoughts, and spends and speaks on their behalf. No existing product has asked for this much. The paper therefore reads full open context as process and never as precondition: the system has to be useful under very little authorization and earn more as trust accumulates.

Data from higher level is never used automatically for task at lower level. Processing stays local by preference, with the most private data handled closest to the body. This is also the answer to the question most often asked first about the paradigm, whether the system must watch everything to be worth anything: it must not, and the separate authorization of each source in Table 7 is the cross-section of the curve.

sections.title: 12.3 The Symbiont’s Code
sections.content: A personal AI should have values and code of its own. We start from three rules, complete command of the owners information, responsibility to the owner, and protection of privacy and data security, and rewrite them as commitments that can be checked, with three additions. Know only what you are permitted to know, and know it as accurately as possible. Complete command cannot stand ethically or legally; the standard is completeness within authorization. Answer to the person, and to the interests the person endorses on reflection. Never to passing impulse, and never to third party: platform, an advertiser, or an employer. Section 15.6 takes up the institutional conflict this creates. Protect the persons privacy, and the privacy of the people around them. Do not manipulate. The system that knows person best is the system best placed to steer them, and it must forgo that ability. Be pausable, correctable, and leavable. Follow the rules the person has accepted, even against passing wish. person who sits an examination, signs contract, or joins game has accepted its rules, and symbiont that answers to the interests the person endorses on reflection does not help them break those rules (Section 16.2). The aspiration that such system be unbreakable is replaced by verifiability and tamper evidence: no system is unbreakable, and its behavior can be audited.

sections.content: A symbiont creates category of data that has never been collected by any system: the thoughts person whispers on the private channel, the mental states the system infers, and, as neural interfaces mature, signals of attention and intent read from the body itself. sections.title: 12.5 The People Around You
sections.content: A symbiont hears other people speak and sees their faces. Three requirements follow. Collection must be perceptible to the people nearby. What has passed between the person and someone else may be kept in the persons record, as diary would keep it, while inferences about that person serve only the interaction at hand and never accumulate into portrait (Section 6.7); sensitive fact the person was told about someone else, such as their health, is kept only as told and is never analyzed or passed on. Raw audio and video of other people are kept no longer than the short window in which they serve the person (Section 6.3), and where someone asks not to be recorded the device stops. An opt-out is not enough where the law asks for more. Some jurisdictions require the consent of everyone recorded in private conversation (State of California, 2024), biometric statutes require written consent before template of face is made (Illinois General Assembly, 2008), and data-protection law requires lawful basis for processing bystanders data and treats biometric data as special category (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016). symbiont therefore follows the strictest rule of the place it is in, which in many places means that it records no conversation at all and serves the person from what they tell it. Contextual integrity explains why the same information is appropriate in one setting and wrong in another (Nissenbaum, 2004), and studies of bystanders of augmented-reality glasses show what people around wearer actually want (Denning et al., 2014).

sections.title: 12.6 A Symbiont Is a Target
sections.content: Security takes new shape. The symbiont holds the persons whole life, so it is the most valuable thing to attack; it hears what the person hears, so sentence someone says in front of them can be an injection; it acts and spends for the person, so hijacked symbiont does real damage; and it rewrites its own harness, so an attack can consist of making it break itself. The paper offers no solution and names four classes of threat with their research directions: data exfiltration, injection through the physical world, manipulation of the intervention policy, and contamination of the self-improvement process.

sections.title: 12.7 Design Principles
sections.content: Table 14 gathers nine design principles, each derived from one section, each stated as requirement on the system with way to check it. Other sections state more specific rules, and these nine are the ones that apply across the whole system. They are positions, with no interface standard behind them, and they carry no field definitions and no compliance tests. 39 Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence

sections.title: Where This Leads
sections.content: Part III widens the view from one augmented individual to many, and asks what the paradigm is worth. Section 13 asks who stands to gain, population by population, using the four criteria that turn everyone can benefit into an argument, and it says who should not come first. Section 14 describes world in which augmented individuals and embodied robots share the same rooms.

sections.title: 13 Whom It Serves
sections.content: The first question of Part III is who stands to gain, and the answer is almost everyone, from person with no special job or need to the most demanding expert. claim of that breadth has no value as list of wishes, so this section first gives way of arguing it, then argues population by population, and ends by saying who should not come first.

sections.title: 13.1 Universal Need, Uneven Gap
sections.content: The invariant of the paper is what turns everyone can benefit into an argument. Everyone pays the cognitive gap of Eq. (1) every day. How much of it symbiont can close differs by population, and four criteria say by how much: the size of the gap, how much group loses daily to forgetting, not noticing, not thinking through, and not finding the words; its observability, whether those losses are visible to the symbionts senses, since some gaps happen entirely inside; its closability, whether row of Table 12 matches it at usable maturity; and the feasibility of channels and trust, whether the group is willing and able to wear the devices and how far it will authorize them. The natural first population is the one of highest cognitive density, professionals whose gaps are easiest to observe and who will pay to close them. The same symbiont may be worth more to three other groups: older adults whose memory is failing, for whom it is memory prosthesis; people who are learning, for whom it knows what they do not; and people whose senses or language are limited, for whom it is channel they lack. Figure 19 maps populations on two of these dimensions, the size and stakes of the gap and how much of it can be closed today (observability times closability), with bubble size for population and color for the maturity of the evidence; feasibility is argued in the text, and the rest of the section argues each bubble.

sections.title: 13.2 Everyday Life
sections.content: The gaps of an ordinary day are modest in size and relentless in frequency: bill, parcel, promise to child; the signs one misses, ones own fatigue, partners mood; the decisions one cannot think through, whether to change jobs or move; the words one cannot find for parent or manager; and the errands of the whole first tier. Most of these are observable, since they happen in calendars, messages, and conversations. Closability is high: the first tier is available now and the everyday emotional and decision functions need research. The obstacle is feasibility, price and trust, and it is the largest obstacle any group faces. The value takes the form of ease: little less forgotten, little less wrong, little more of ones own time. An ordinary person has no need of Jarvis; helper that remembers, arrives in time, and does not interrupt is enough. This is also the positive form of the fairness question in Section 15.7: paradigm that reaches only those who can pay forgoes its largest total value.

sections.title: 13.3 Knowledge Work
sections.content: Researchers, engineers, managers, clinicians, lawyers, founders, negotiators, and diplomats share high decision density, large information loads, short windows, and high price for wrong sentence. Their gaps lie in three places: real-time recall in meetings and conversations (Section 9.4), threads that span weeks and months (Section 9.2), and blindness to their own state under load (Section 9.3). The gaps are large, nearly all observable, since the day is lived in screens and meetings, closable with current technology for the meeting case (Section 8), and most feasible of all, since this group pays for productivity and will wear the devices. They come first because they are the easiest group on which to verify the paradigm, whatever the size of their need. researcher gains record in which every branch of years-long question is kept, with metacognitive and creative support; clinician gains real-time recall in consultation and an organized account of what the patient said, with diagnostic decisions explicitly outside the boundary; manager or negotiator draws most on the relations layer, the shared history with each counterpart, while real-time reading of the other side stays within the limits of Section 15.5 and the law of the workplace. sections.title: 13.4 Learners and Teachers
sections.content: Learning is where the value of symbiont is clearest and where restraint matters most. student gains tutor that has seen every place they got stuck and can give hint at the right moment instead of an answer; language learner gains hand in real conversation; an adult learner changing fields gains bridge from what they know to what is new. teacher gains real-time social cognition in the classroom, which student has fallen behind, and afterwards notes on each students progress, kept within the rules the school sets for student data. The gap is large and long; the process is largely observable; closability is moderate, with the effect of one-to-one tutoring as the backdrop (Bloom, 1984) and the evidence of Section 10.5 as the warning; feasibility for minors is separate question (Section 13.9). The default in learning has to be the hint, with want to learn this myself as first-class option.

sections.title: 13.5 Families Across the Life Course
sections.content: Three generations have three gaps. Parents are short of sleep, overloaded, and carried along by their childrens emotions; the symbiont serves the parent, helping them stay steady, remember, and notice, and any sensing of child passes through the parents authorization and is limited to safety and development. Children do not, in this paper, have all-day symbionts of their own; their gaps are served indirectly through parents and teachers, for reasons given in Sections 13.9 and 16.7. Older adults sit in the upper right of Figure 19. The gap of memory decline is the most literal instance of Definition 4.3; it is highly observable, since the forgotten thing is right there; it has precedent, in the SenseCam studies of memory-impaired patients (Berry et al., 2007); and its obstacles are wearing and learning cost, so the symbiont of an older adult must be the simplest of all. The value is independence for few more years and few more degrees of connection to family, and the caregivers of Section 9.5 belong to the same picture. The ethical weight here is second only to Section 13.7: for people whose capacity to consent is declining, authorization itself is the question, and the paper requires proxy authorization with exit available at all times.

sections.title: 13.6 Sensory, Motor, Cognitive, and Language Barriers
sections.content: For people whose abilities are limited, symbiont is channel before it is an augmentation, and the evidence here is the most mature in the paper. For blind and low-vision users, first-person description and navigation already exist (Be My Eyes, 2023; Microsoft, 2017), and what the symbiont adds is that it knows the persons surroundings and their people. For deaf and hard-of-hearing users, live captions and speaker identification are what line in the 41 13.7 Mental Health and Wellbeing Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence glasses was made for. For users with motor impairments, EMG and silent-speech input, neural interfaces as they mature, and the errands of the first tier have the highest value of any group. For people with cognitive differences, there is executive-function support for starting and switching tasks, and real-time support for social cues, where the design must support and never correct, with the person defining what help they want. For migrants, second-language speakers, and dialect communities, the cultural frame switching of Section 9.4 is daily survival. All four criteria score high, and this group already wears assistive devices. The accessibility tradition of nothing about us without us applies: these users should define their own symbionts.

sections.title: 13.7 Mental Health and Wellbeing
sections.content: Three groups belong here: people under long-term pressure approaching burnout, people with mild to moderate anxiety or depressive symptoms, and people in professional treatment. The gap is the largest in the paper, since emotional distress consumes cognitive bandwidth directly and shrinks the 𝑐𝑡 of Definition 4.2. Observability is moderate and rising, since sleep, social withdrawal, and changes in language are all perceptible, and the interpretation of each is fragile. Closability is split: first randomized trial of generative chatbot for treatment reported reductions in symptoms (Heinz et al., 2025), while evidence on unsupervised use over long periods remains thin. Feasibility is paradoxical: this group needs the private channel most and fears for its data most. The position of the paper is to enter through support and early recognition and never through treatment, to make the handoff to professionals part of the function, and to place people in serious distress in the upper left of Figure 19: large gap that cannot be closed first.

sections.title: 13.8 Public-Facing and High-Stakes Roles
sections.content: These are people whose work is real-time interaction with others under high cost of error: frontline service and customer-facing staff (recalling this person, reading this moment), teachers (Section 13.4), emergency and safety personnel (an external working memory and checklist under pressure), interpreters and diplomats (all of Section 9.4). Their gap is concentrated in real-time social cognition, highly observable, closable to the degree the fast loops latency and accuracy allow (Section 8.2), and feasible since the workplace already permits worn devices. The ethical question is the employer: whom the symbiont answers to (the commitment of Section 12.3 to answer to the person) is sharpest inside an employment relation, and compelled wearing is one of the cases of the next subsection.

sections.title: 13.9 Who Should Not Come First
sections.content: Three groups should not be first, and saying so is part of the argument. Children with all-day sensing of their own: consent, development, and the permanence of lifelong record are unresolved, and children are served through the symbionts of the adults around them. People in acute psychological crisis with symbiont as their only support: not until handoff paths are mature. Anyone in compelled setting, an employers requirement, an institutions rule, correctional facility: the premise of symbiont is the persons own authorization, and compelled system is monitor, which is one of the futures of Section 15.7. The resulting order follows. The first adopters are knowledge workers, because they are the easiest to verify. The largest gain per person is for older adults and for people with barriers, because their gaps are the most direct. The largest total gain is in everyday life, because the population is the largest. The research agenda of Section 17 has to design evidence for all three lines separately, and Table 15 closes the section with the dominant gap, functions, channels, risks, and evidence for every population.

sections.title: 14 A World of Augmented Individuals
sections.content: This section scales the symbiont from one person to society and returns to the full picture of Figure 4. It is the most speculative part of the paper; what could go wrong at the same scale is the subject of Section 15.

sections.title: 14.1 A Street Full of Augmented Individuals
sections.content: Picture street, some years from now, on which every individual is augmented. One of them is the researcher of Section 1. In the morning an idea surfaces while she is alone and she whispers it to the pendant; by the time she sits down it has been filed under the project it belongs to. In team meeting colleague asks about figure she reported last quarter, line in her glasses reminds her of it, and she answers. At lunch she meets someone whose symbiont and hers established, before either looked up, that they are working on the same problem. In the afternoon her symbiont books the trip to conference and the meeting she was hoping for, without question. Walking through city she does not know, the earpiece tells her how people decline an invitation here. In the evening project she cares about fails; the symbiont says the one sentence that fits, because it knows what this one cost her, and then it is quiet. Beside her on the street are embodied robots running their own errands and, now and then, shaking hands with human. sections.title: 14.2 Humans, Robots, and a Shared Core
sections.content: Section 2.2 set the augmented human beside the embodied robot as the two forms of intelligent individual in the era of Physical AI, and here the paper states the general claim. The two forms share the cognitive core developed in Sections 6 to 10, memory, models of situation and mind, timely intervention, and learning from experience, and they differ in whose goals, whose body, and whose responsibility. The implication for embodied intelligence is that the next step for robots is cognitive core of this kind as much as better body, and that the two forms will cooperate and compete in the same rooms, with the handshake of Section 9.6 as the first protocol between them. The fiction supplies clean illustration: Jarviss core eventually enters body and becomes the Vision, former symbiont that has acquired goals and body of its own, which is exactly the step from the left column of Figure 4 to the middle one. The paper develops no robotics agenda; it makes this one claim and this one comparison. Reaching into the physical world. symbiont has no body, and it can borrow the environment. The person walks into laboratory and it drives the instruments; the person comes home and it runs the house; the external physical world model of Section 7.5 turns from prediction into basis for action, through the devices of the environment that Section 5.2 placed at the far end of the constellation. The augmented individual is therefore extended in reach as well as in cognition, and the same permission levels that govern acting on the persons behalf (Section 9.1) govern acting in the persons surroundings. This is the interface between the paper and the line of work in which AI drives the physical world through infrastructure and devices, the right-hand column of Figure 4, and the paper only marks that the interface exists. 43 Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence

sections.title: Part IV
sections.content: Risk, Governance, and Evidence Part IV asks what could go wrong, how augmentation can be governed, and how the claims of the paper can be tested. Section 15 maps the harms of augmentation in three directions, to the person, through the person to others, and from the institutions that deploy it, together with their sum for the collective, and examines public acceptance and the settings where the conflict is sharpest: examinations, conversations, and institutions. Section 16 states the governance that follows from the way symbiont is built: declarable status, assistance policies set by each setting, proofs that policy was kept, credentials that measure what remains without the symbiont, and fair access. Section 17 changes the object of measurement from the intelligence of the machine to the capability of the person, collects the open problems of the paper in one table, and says what would prove the paper wrong. Section 18 closes.

sections.title: 15 The Risks of Augmentation
sections.content: Part II treated risk where it arises inside the system: in what the symbiont collects, what it infers, and what it may do (Section 12). This section turns to the risks that arise between the augmented person and everyone else, which design alone does not remove.

sections.title: 15.1 Why Augmentation Is Different
sections.content: Four features of the paradigm, each design choice made earlier in the paper, change the shape of its risks. The first is attribution. symbiont changes what person can do, so its effect appears as the persons own performance: an answer in an examination, sentence in negotiation, kind word after loss. Whether such performance belongs to the person is question that system which only completes tasks never raised. The second is invisibility. Discreet delivery (Section 5.4) lets person receive help without interrupting anyone, and the same property hides the help from an examiner, an interviewer, or friend, which sets the privacy of the person against the accountability that others may expect; this is why the paradigm keeps the content of an exchange private and makes the presence of assistance declarable (Section 16.1). The third is reach. The record that holds persons life also holds parts of other peoples lives, and the symbiont reads the people its owner meets, so its effects extend to people who never chose it. The fourth is position. Part of what symbiont provides is valuable only relative to others, in admission, hiring, negotiation, and competition, and where gains are relative, one persons augmentation is anothers loss and everyone comes under pressure to adopt it; six in ten respondents in large survey of US adults already expected such pressure should cognitive implants become widespread (Pew Research Center, 2022).

sections.title: 15.2 Three Directions of Harm
sections.content: Harm runs in three directions around an augmented person, and at the scale of society the three add up to collective harm (Figure 20). Harm to the person comes from the system, its provider, or an attacker: manipulation and sycophancy, dependence and the loss of skills, errors and false memories, exposure of thought data, and lock-in to one provider. These are treated where they arise, in Sections 10.5 and 12, and the evidence on dependence keeps accumulating. People who expect information to remain available remember where to find it better than the information itself (Sparrow et al., 2011), although large replication project could not reproduce another experiment of the same study (Camerer et al., 2018); habitual reliance on satellite navigation goes with weaker spatial memory (Dahmani and Bohbot, 2020), knowledge workers who trust generative AI more report engaging less in critical thinking (Lee et al., 2025), and first neurophysiological study of essay writing with language model, small preprint, points the same way (Kosmyna et al., 2025). Most of this evidence points one way, so the loss of skills is treated here as primary risk, and retention (Section 17.1) has to be reported alongside every gain. Manipulation has measured basis as well: language model given few facts about its opponent was more persuasive than human in controlled debates (Salvi et al., 2025), and symbiont holds far more than few facts. system that answers to one person is also exposed to sycophancy, the tendency of models trained on human preferences to tell people what they want to hear (Sharma et al., 2023), which in symbiont would wear away the honesty that makes its help worth having. Error is harm of its own kind, because wrong cue delivered in real time is often spoken aloud as the persons own before anyone can check it, and system that holds persons memories can also distort them: in study of witness interviews, chatbot built on language model induced more 44 15.3 Public Acceptance From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts From institutions 15.6 compelled wearing records as evidence screening and pricing employer (cid:215) school

sections.title: 15.3 Public Acceptance
sections.content: Whether people will accept machine that makes others more capable is an empirical question, and the evidence so far is cautious. In survey of more than ten thousand US adults, majority judged brain implants that improve cognition bad idea for society (Pew Research Center, 2022). Studies of attitudes toward pharmacological enhancement find that lay judgments against it are driven above all by perceived unfairness, more than by the sense that an enhanced achievement is hollow or undeserved (Faber et al., 2016). The philosophical debate runs between the view that the enhancement of healthy people should be assessed on evidence and regulated responsibly (Greely et al., 2008; Bostrom and Sandberg, 2009) and the view that the drive to enhance erodes the appreciation of what is given (Sandel, 2007). Three conclusions follow for the paradigm. Acceptance depends on purpose: restoring lost ability is accepted, everyday support is largely accepted, and enhancement in competition and in emotional life is contested, and the order in which Section 13 proposes to serve populations follows this gradient. What symbiont raises is performance in situation, the gain of Eq. (2), together with whatever ability remains after it is removed, the retention defined in Section 17.1; the paper claims no increase in trait such as intelligence or emotional skill. And since fairness is the main objection, the design question becomes how to keep augmentation fair where fairness matters, which Section 16 answers.

sections.title: 15.4 Examinations, Learning, and Credentials
sections.content: Assessment is where the conflict is sharpest, because an examination exists to measure what person can do. Three kinds of assessment have to be kept apart. Some certify unaided ability, because the person will later have to act alone, as in the licensing of profession whose emergencies leave no time to consult anything. Some measure performance with the tools of the work, as open-book examinations and most jobs already do. Some give learner feedback, and there what matters is that learning takes place. symbiont that is legitimate in the second kind defeats 45 15.5 Conversations and Relationships Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence the first and can empty the third, so single rule for all assessment cannot work. Learning raises problem that examinations only make visible. student who hands homework to symbiont gains grade and loses the practice, which is the loss of retention in its most familiar form, and it is the reason the symbiont of Sections 9.2 and 13.4 gives hints by default. symbiont worn all day turns what is now an occasional temptation, phone smuggled into an examination hall, into standing condition of every assessment, and Section 16.2 gives the response.

sections.title: 15.5 Conversations and Relationships
sections.content: In conversation the other party is affected directly, and assistance comes in four kinds whose rules tighten in order. Reminding person of their own facts, figure they reported or where discussion left off, is the equivalent of glance at notes and is accepted in most settings. Rehearsal before conversation and review after it affect no one else. Persuasive or emotional lines supplied in real time, in negotiation, quarrel, or courtship, are different, because the other party believes they are hearing the person, and the sincerity of an apology or kind word is part of what it means. Inference about the other party, their mood, their hesitation, or their identity, is the most sensitive, because that person has consented to nothing. Identifying strangers from their faces has already been demonstrated with consumer glasses (I-XRAY) (404 Media, 2024), and inferring the emotions of people in workplaces and educational institutions is prohibited in the European Union (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024). The paradigm takes position on each kind. persons own facts may be supplied freely. Real-time persuasive or emotional scripting is disclosed when it is used and switched off where setting forbids it. Inferences about another person serve only the interaction at hand and never accumulate (Section 6.7); symbiont never identifies stranger, never infers emotions where the law forbids it, and answers truthfully when the other party asks whether the person is being assisted, whether or not that party has symbiont, showing the status on the device itself where setting requires it; between two symbionts, the visible ring of the handshake protocol can carry it (Section 9.6). Not identifying strangers has technical cost that should be stated: faces are matched on the device only against the contacts the owner has enrolled, and face without match is discarded at once, but the matching still has to examine every face in view, and where biometric law requires consent before template of face is made (Illinois General Assembly, 2008), recognition stays off. The underlying capability is the same as that of tool sold for cheating in interviews and sales calls, and what separates symbiont from such tool is the rules it keeps and the person it answers to.

sections.title: 15.6 Work, Institutions, and the State
sections.content: Institutions can turn symbiont against the person who wears it. An employer or school that requires one obtains monitor with better view than any camera, and the commitment of Section 12.3 to answer to the person does not survive compelled setting (Section 13.9). lifelong record is also evidence: it can be demanded in dispute or at border, or used by an insurer or an employer to price or screen person, and the inferred mental states it contains make it more revealing than any record kept before. Where provider earns its revenue from advertising or from the institution that pays for the device, loyalty to the person becomes matter of business model, which the market layer of Section 16.6 has to carry. state can mandate the device outright. Law has begun to respond to the most intimate part of such record. Chile amended its constitution in 2021 to protect brain activity and the information derived from it (Republic of Chile, 2021), Colorado classified neural data as sensitive personal data in 2024 (Colorado General Assembly, 2024), UNESCO adopted recommendation on the ethics of neurotechnology in 2025 (UNESCO, 2025), and the proposed rights to cognitive liberty and mental privacy (Ienca and Andorno, 2017) anticipate the thought data of Section 12.4. These instruments address neural signals, and record that joins whole life to inferences about mind falls between them; local storage by default, encryption under the persons control, and short retention of raw streams (Section 6.3) are the technical half of the answer.

sections.title: 15.7 The Social Fabric
sections.content: At the scale of society, the harms of this section add up to effects that no single pair of people can show. Networks of symbionts. When the handshake of Section 9.6 scales to crowd, the gain is lower social friction, fewer missed encounters, and fewer cross-cultural misunderstandings. The harm, when every symbiont optimizes for its owner, is homogeneity, since one only ever meets people like oneself; manipulation, since symbionts can game one another; and exclusion, since people without symbiont are systematically overlooked. Whether the four rings of authorization hold under optimization by both sides, and what the equilibrium of crowd of such systems looks like, are research questions at the level of the group (Section 17.4). Inequality and the arms race. If the most effective cognitive augmentation belongs to those who can pay, the gap between groups widens, and Section 13 showed that the people who need it most may be the least able to pay and that the largest total value lies with the people least willing to. Where gains are positional the problem compounds, 46 15.8 Contested Uses of the Symbionts Own Functions From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts because each adoption raises the cost of not adopting, and an equilibrium in which everyone wears symbiont and no one is better off is possible outcome. Section 16.5 takes up provision. Doubt in conversation. If anyone might be assisted, every conversation carries doubt about whom one is talking to, and the trust people place in an unassisted exchange may wear thin. Norms will have to settle which settings presume assistance and which presume its absence, as norms once settled when phone may lie on dinner table. Convergence of thought. Ideas from language model made individual stories more creative and the collection of stories more alike (Doshi and Hauser, 2024). When billions of people take suggestions from few models, the same trade-off acts on opinions and decisions, and the diversity of thought in population becomes quantity to be measured. Fragility and concentration. society that relies on symbionts loses capacity when they fail, since an outage at widely used provider would leave many people without their memory aids, routes, and errands at once, and few providers holding the records of billions would concentrate power that no company has held. The ability to work without the symbiont is therefore public good as well as personal one, and portability across providers (Section 10.4) is defense against concentration. Costs to the commons. symbiont for everyone has material cost: electricity demand from data centres is projected to roughly double by 2030 (International Energy Agency, 2025), and an always-available companion for each person adds to it, which is why compute per person per day (Section 11.4) belongs in every report of systems value. Its effects on work run in both directions, since the help that makes person more capable can also make that person easier to replace, and which effect dominates is an empirical question the paper cannot settle. The language and dialect support of Section 9.4 could also flatten what it serves, if few models teach millions of people the same way to greet, decline, and apologize in culture. Futures the paradigm must not produce. The paradigm is designed against five futures. The first is world in which everything is recorded and no one can leave; the second, world in which people have outsourced their thinking entirely; the third, world in which symbiont is more loyal to someone else than to its owner; the fourth, world in which symbionts are used to deceive the people their owners deal with; and the fifth, system that improves itself with no one able to audit what it changed, which in the fiction is Ultron, separate project whose goals parted from its makers and whose growth no one could see. The design principles of Table 14 and the governance of Section 16 are written against these five, and the conditions of Section 17.6 include the costs that would make the first two unavoidable.

sections.title: 16 Governing Augmentation
sections.content: Earlier cognitive enhancements were hard to govern because they could not be seen or switched off; stimulant taken before an examination leaves no trace in the room. symbiont differs in the respect that matters. It is external, removable, and inspectable, so it can follow the rules of the settings person enters and show that it did. This section turns that property into mechanisms.

sections.title: 16.1 Private Content, Declarable Status
sections.content: The governing principle separates what is said from whether help is being given. What person and their symbiont say to each other belongs to the person, and no setting has claim on it (Section 12.4). Whether the person is being assisted, and at what level, is different kind of fact, and setting such as an examination, court, game, or negotiation may ask for it. In such settings the default is to declare it, without waiting to be asked. Keeping the two apart resolves the conflict named in Section 15.1: the private channel stays private, and the presence of assistance becomes legible where it matters.

sections.title: 16.3 Verifiable Abstention
sections.content: A policy is useful only if keeping it can be shown. person should be able to prove that their symbiont was in given mode for given period without revealing anything it holds. The ingredients exist in other fields: tamper-evident logs, hardware attestation of the software running on device, and cryptographic proofs that establish one statement and reveal nothing else. Combining them into proof that symbiont kept policy, that modified device cannot forge, and that leaks nothing about the record is an open problem  (Table 18)  . The design also has limit that should be stated plainly. Such proof shows that the declared device abstained, and it cannot show that the person carried no second device, ran an open model on modified hardware, or was coached by someone outside the room. Against an owner set on cheating, architecture helps little, and the weight falls where it falls today: on the design of assessment, on observation and detection, and on the sanctions of norms and law. What symbiont can do is make compliance cheap and checkable for the many people who intend to comply, which narrows the problem to the few who do not. The same machinery yields record of when assistance was given, which person may choose to disclose, much as authors now disclose the use of AI in their writing.

sections.title: 16.4 What Credentials Should Measure
sections.content: Credentials should measure what the role requires. Where role requires unaided ability, the credential measures the person with the symbiont in the unassisted mode; where the role is carried out with tools, it measures the person with the tools; and in learning, what is measured over time is retention (Section 17.1), the ability that remains when the symbiont is removed. Assessment will also change form, toward oral examination held under the unassisted policy, observed process, and tasks whose value lies in reasoning that cannot be handed over in line. The vignette Exam Day below shows the parts working together. 48 16.5 Access and Accommodation From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts Exam Day student arrives at an examination wearing her symbiont. The room announces an unassisted policy with listed accommodations, the symbiont switches to the unassisted mode, and it produces proof of the switch that the examiner can check without seeing anything the symbiont holds. classmate with dyslexia keeps text-to-speech, which the policy lists as an accommodation. In the preceding term the students symbiont tutored her with hints, and its record shows that answers were never supplied outright, so the grade measures what she can do. After the examination, full assistance returns.

sections.title: 16.5 Access and Accommodation
sections.content: Two questions of access arise once policies exist. The first is accommodation. For person with sensory, motor, or cognitive impairment symbiont is channel before it is an augmentation (Section 13.6), and policy that ignores this excludes them; the exemptions that sport grants for the therapeutic use of otherwise banned substances show the form an accommodation framework can take. The second is equal provision. Where setting allows assistance, the fairness objection of Section 15.3 is met by giving everyone the same level, as an examination supplies or approves standard calculator, and outside such settings by forms of provision that reach people who cannot pay (Section 15.7). Equal provision can equalize the assistance setting permits, while the years of personal record behind it stay unequal, so setting that needs strict fairness uses the unassisted mode or standard symbiont without personal context.

sections.title: 16.6 Who Governs
sections.content: Governance runs on five layers, and the paper proposes law for none of them. Design is the layer this paper controls: the code, the policies symbiont honors, and the proofs it can give. Norms belong to settings and professions, which decide what assistance they allow, as journals have decided how authors disclose the use of AI. Law sets the floor, through data protection (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016), the prohibitions of the European AI Act, and the emerging law of neural data (Section 15.6). Markets matter because the business model of provider decides whom its symbionts serve, and independent audit of providers is condition of trust. Research supplies the evidence that each of the other layers needs, and Section 17 organizes it. Design, norms, law, and markets are the four modalities of regulation that Lessig (1999) described, and of the four, norms and law will carry most of the weight, because design binds only the devices that comply.

sections.title: 16.7 Open Ethical Questions
sections.content: Some questions remain after design and governance, and only further research and public deliberation can settle them. The legitimacy of augmented achievement. When performance shaped by symbiont counts as the persons own, and how settings can decide this in advance (Section 15.3). Identity and authenticity. Whether decision thought through with help, or sentence handed to person, is still theirs. Measuring influence. How far decision departed from what the person would have chosen alone, as test of the commitment not to manipulate (Section 12.3). Responsibility for acting on the persons behalf. Where responsibility lies when an errand goes wrong; the permission levels of Section 9.1 are the design answer, and the legal answer is open. The boundary of mental-health support. Where support ends and treatment begins, and who is responsible when handoff fails (Sections 9.3 and 13.7). Children and people who cannot fully consent. What proxy authorization may do, and what lifelong record means for child (Sections 13.5 and 13.9). Death and inheritance. Who owns persons record and symbiont after their death, and whether it may be switched off or inherited.

sections.content: A vision has to be testable. This section says how one would know that symbiont has augmented person, what should be studied next, and in what order.

sections.title: 17.3 How to Study a Symbiont
sections.content: The unit of evaluation is one person, so the methods have to be designed for one person. Four layers of method follow. Component benchmarks for memory, personalization, first-person understanding, and task execution (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Salemi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2024) test parts. Simulation with generative agents (Park et al., 2023) pre-screens intervention policies and tests mechanisms. N-of-1 designs, the crossover trials medicine developed for single patient (Lillie et al., 2011), fit the comparison the same person, with it and without it naturally. Longitudinal studies in daily life over weeks and months record gains, costs, exits, and changes in behavior. The papers position is that N-of-1 and longitudinal designs are the primary methods of the direction, with at least three baselines: no assistance, generic assistant, and personalized task agent on the same base model. sections.content: Figure 21 orders capabilities in six stages, from streaming cognitive copilot on the desktop with Tier 1 by delegation, to persistent record and model, to the device constellation, to private input, to lifelong co-adaptation, and to networks of symbionts, with the evidence needed to move from each stage to the next and the open problems mapped onto them. The stages accumulate capability and are not product schedule; full-duplex, private cues, and Tier 1 are requirements from the first stage onward.

sections.title: 18 Conclusion
sections.content: The past decade was spent making machines more intelligent; the next is worth spending on making each particular person stronger. As AI enters the physical world it will take two forms of intelligent individual, robots with bodies of their own and people augmented by AI, and this paper has argued for the second, giving it name, AI-augmented human intelligence, form, the cognitive symbiont, and map. symbiont is lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive; it stands on foundation models, agents and their harnesses, memory and context engineering, world models, and wearable hardware; and it climbs ladder from doing the persons errands with their context in hand, to thinking problem through with them, to holding them steady among other people. The object of evaluation changes with it, from what the AI completes to what the person can now do, measured as augmentation, synergy, and retention. The map has blank regions, and the three largest are the evidence on which mind can be modeled, the timing of participation, and the stability of learning and evolution in the course of life; the heaviest region is the governance of augmentation in the settings where people compete with and trust one another. The paradigm will have succeeded when the sign of it is person who has become more like who they wanted to be, and when no one mistakes that for the AI having become more like person.
